questions.hint: Think about helping people understand how an AI system reaches or supports an output.

options.text: Methods and practices that make AI outputs and behavior understandable to people
A type of AI that never makes mistakes
A technique that removes the need for human review
A guarantee that every model decision is simple

summary: XAI makes an AI system's behavior, outputs, or decisions understandable to relevant people.
An explanation can help evaluate a result, but does not prove that the result is correct.

questions.questionText: Why is explainability important in AI systems?
questions.hint: People need more than a prediction when they must decide whether to rely on it.

options.text: It helps people assess, challenge, and appropriately use AI outputs
It guarantees that the model's training data is unbiased
It makes every AI system legally compliant automatically
It prevents the model from needing monitoring

summary: Explanations help users and reviewers understand why an output may be relevant and what limits apply.
Explainability complements, rather than replaces, testing, monitoring, and governance.

questions.hint: Consider the difficulty of evaluating a result when the system's behavior is opaque.

options.text: The difficulty of understanding and evaluating how AI systems produce outputs
The need to provide data to an AI model
The computational cost of training all models
The need to define a system's intended use

summary: XAI addresses opacity by providing useful information about model behavior and individual results.
It does not eliminate other challenges such as poor data, model errors, or unclear objectives.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between AI, ML, Deep Learning, and Generative AI?
questions.hint: Think of these terms as overlapping categories rather than four unrelated technologies.

options.text: AI is the broad field; ML learns from data; deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks; generative AI creates new content
They are four names for the same specific algorithm
Generative AI is a subset of deep learning, which is a subset of ML, but AI excludes all three
Machine learning is broader than AI and does not use data

summary: AI is the broad area of creating systems that perform intelligent tasks; ML is one approach within AI.
Deep learning is a family of ML methods based on neural networks, and generative AI describes systems that generate content; categories can overlap.

questions.questionText: Why are modern AI models often called "black boxes"?
questions.hint: A model can have many complex internal computations that are not easy to describe in plain language.

options.text: Their internal computations can be too complex or opaque for people to follow directly
Their source code is always secret
They accept only encrypted input
They cannot produce explanations of any kind

summary: The black-box label describes difficulty interpreting a model's internal behavior, especially in large or complex models.
It does not necessarily mean the model is proprietary or that no explanation method can be applied.

questions.questionText: What are the risks of non-explainable AI?
questions.hint: Think about unfair outcomes, mistakes that go unnoticed, and difficulty assigning responsibility.

options.text: Errors or harmful patterns may be harder to detect
People may be unable to challenge an important decision effectively
It guarantees that decisions will be biased
Audits and accountability can become more difficult

summary: Opacity can make errors, unfair effects, and responsibility harder to investigate or contest.
A non-explainable system is not automatically biased, but its behavior may be harder to assess.

questions.hint: Trust should be based on evidence and appropriate expectations, not simply confidence.

options.text: It gives people information to judge a result's basis, limits, and suitability
It persuades users to accept every AI recommendation
It makes a model's output true by describing it
It replaces independent evaluation with user confidence

summary: Clear, evidence-based explanations can support calibrated trust: relying on the system where appropriate and questioning it where needed.
The aim is not blind trust or automatic acceptance.

questions.hint: Transparency concerns how much relevant information about a system is made available.

options.text: Making relevant information about an AI system, its design, data, or operation available
Showing every internal model computation to every user
Publishing source code regardless of privacy or security
Explaining only the final prediction

summary: Transparency is about disclosure of relevant information about a system and its operation.
What should be disclosed depends on the audience, context, and legitimate confidentiality or security needs.

questions.hint: Ask whether a person can make sense of the model's behavior or structure.

options.text: The degree to which a person can understand how a model behaves or reaches outputs
The accuracy of a model on a test set
The process of encrypting model parameters
A synonym for publishing training data

summary: Interpretability concerns how readily people can understand a model's operation or behavior.
It is related to explainability, but an explanation may also be generated for a model that is not inherently interpretable.

questions.hint: Traceability lets an investigator follow the path from inputs and actions to an outcome.

options.text: The ability to follow relevant data, model versions, steps, and decisions through a system
The ability to predict every future model output
The process of hiding a model's operational history
A score that measures only model accuracy

summary: Traceability connects inputs, system versions, intermediate actions, and outcomes so they can be reconstructed.
Good records support audits and investigations, subject to privacy and retention controls.

questions.hint: An AI system cannot take organizational responsibility for its use.

options.text: People and organizations are responsible for AI systems and their impacts
The model independently accepts legal responsibility for its outputs
A model's ability to explain itself without human involvement
A guarantee that every output can be reversed

summary: Accountability means identifiable people or organizations answer for how AI is developed, deployed, and used.
An explanation can support accountability but does not transfer responsibility to the model.

questions.questionText: How are transparency and explainability different?
questions.hint: One is about information being available; the other is about making behavior or an output understandable.

options.text: Transparency discloses relevant system information; explainability helps people understand a system's behavior or result
Transparency applies only to open-source models; explainability applies only to closed models
They are identical terms and always mean publishing source code
Explainability concerns data privacy, while transparency concerns accuracy

summary: Transparency makes relevant details available, while explainability provides understandable reasons or accounts of behavior.
They reinforce one another but are not interchangeable.

questions.questionText: Why is explainability critical in regulated industries?
questions.hint: Organizations may need to justify consequential decisions and demonstrate appropriate controls.

options.text: It can help organizations justify decisions, investigate outcomes, and demonstrate governance
It automatically satisfies every legal requirement
It allows regulated organizations to avoid keeping records
It guarantees that regulators will approve a model

summary: Explanations and records can support oversight, dispute handling, and evidence of responsible processes.
Legal obligations depend on jurisdiction and use; XAI alone does not ensure compliance.

questions.questionText: What business value does explainable AI provide?
questions.hint: Consider how understanding an output can help teams use, improve, and defend a system.

options.text: It can support adoption, troubleshooting, risk control, and better-informed decisions
It guarantees immediate cost savings for every project
It eliminates the need to measure business outcomes
It makes all data and models publicly accessible

summary: When explanations fit the audience and task, they can help teams diagnose issues and use outputs responsibly.
Value should be measured in context rather than assumed.

questions.questionText: How does XAI support responsible AI?
questions.hint: Responsible systems need ways to scrutinize behavior and correct problems.

options.text: It can help people assess fairness, safety, limitations, and accountability
It removes the need for privacy and security safeguards
It ensures that humans never need to review outputs
It guarantees that model decisions are ethical

summary: XAI can give stakeholders evidence to assess and challenge system behavior as part of responsible AI practices.
It is one part of a broader program that includes governance, testing, security, and human oversight.

questions.hint: These systems create new content based on patterns learned from data and the provided context.

options.text: AI that generates new content such as text, images, audio, or code
AI that only sorts records into fixed categories
A database that returns only exact stored copies
Any software that uses a graphical interface

summary: Generative AI produces content in response to inputs, often by learning patterns from training data.
Generated content can be plausible without being factually correct.

questions.questionText: How does Generative AI differ from traditional AI?
questions.hint: Compare creating content with tasks such as classification, ranking, or prediction.

options.text: Generative AI creates new content, while many traditional AI systems predict, classify, rank, or detect
Generative AI never uses machine learning
Traditional AI always produces explanations, while generative AI cannot
There is no difference in the types of tasks they perform

summary: Generative systems produce content; other AI systems often estimate labels, scores, or decisions.
The distinction is about common tasks, not a strict separation of underlying methods.

questions.hint: They are trained on large collections of text and work with sequences of tokens.

options.text: Neural language models trained at scale to process and generate text
Search engines that always retrieve verified facts
Rule lists written entirely by human experts
Small databases that store one answer per question

summary: LLMs learn statistical patterns in language and generate or transform text based on context.
Their fluency does not mean they have verified every claim they produce.

questions.questionText: Why are LLMs difficult to explain?
questions.hint: Think about their scale, distributed representations, and context-dependent token generation.

options.text: Their many interacting parameters and computation steps make behavior hard to summarize faithfully
They never use input context when generating text
Their training data is always fully known and traceable
They use only one simple human-readable rule

summary: Large neural networks encode patterns across many parameters and layers, so a short explanation of an output is challenging.
Available explanation methods provide partial evidence, not a complete map of internal cognition.

questions.hint: Transformers combine many layers and attention operations over token representations.

options.text: Many interacting layers, attention heads, parameters, and token representations contribute to outputs
They contain no learned parameters
Each output is determined by one directly readable rule
They process every word independently with no context

summary: Transformer outputs arise from many learned operations that combine contextual information across tokens.
Visualizing one component, such as attention, does not by itself explain the full model.

questions.questionText: What is emergent behavior in LLMs?
questions.hint: Some capabilities appear as models scale, even when they were not explicitly programmed as separate features.

options.text: A capability or behavior that appears from interactions in a model, sometimes becoming more apparent at scale
A feature that was manually coded as a fixed rule
An error caused only by a broken network connection
A guarantee that larger models are always safer

summary: Emergent behavior refers to capabilities or patterns arising from complex learned interactions, often observed as scale changes.
The term does not imply that a capability is reliable, beneficial, or truly unpredictable.

questions.questionText: Why can GenAI produce unexpected outputs?
questions.hint: Generation depends on learned patterns, prompt context, and sometimes sampling.

options.text: It generates from probabilistic learned patterns and may interpret ambiguous context in unintended ways
It always looks up one fixed answer in a trusted database
Its output is manually written in advance for every prompt
It is unable to use information from its prompt

summary: Outputs depend on learned distributions, prompting, decoding settings, and system context.
Unexpected results should be anticipated and checked, especially in consequential uses.

questions.hint: A fluent answer may sound confident but lack factual support.

options.text: Generated claims that are false, unsupported, or not grounded in reliable evidence
Any answer that contains a new sentence
A model's correct refusal to answer
A type of database index used by an LLM

summary: A hallucination is generated content that is inaccurate or unsupported, despite possibly sounding plausible.
The term is commonly used for language models but the same concern applies to other generative systems.

questions.hint: An LLM is optimized to generate likely text, not automatically to verify every statement.

options.text: The model can generate plausible continuations without reliable evidence or a fact-checking mechanism
Every answer is copied from an authoritative live source
Hallucinations occur only when users type spelling errors
The model's confidence score always confirms factual truth

summary: Language-model training encourages likely continuations, which may not correspond to verified facts.
Gaps in context, ambiguous prompts, or weak retrieval can raise the chance of unsupported claims.

questions.questionText: How can explainability reduce hallucination risks?
questions.hint: Expose evidence and uncertainty so a person can check claims rather than relying on fluent phrasing.

options.text: Show supporting sources, disclose uncertainty, and make claims easier to verify
Add confident-sounding reasoning to every answer
Hide retrieved evidence to avoid confusing users
Treat every generated explanation as proof

summary: Grounding, citations, and uncertainty indicators can make unsupported claims easier to notice and investigate.
An explanation does not eliminate hallucinations; source quality and claim verification still matter.

questions.questionText: Why is explainability more challenging in GenAI than traditional ML?
questions.hint: Generative systems produce long, context-sensitive content rather than one fixed label or score.

options.text: A response can contain many claims and tokens influenced by complex context and decoding choices
Traditional ML models always reveal their full reasoning
Generative models do not take inputs
GenAI produces only one numeric prediction

summary: A generated response may have many parts with different evidence, and its wording can vary with context and sampling.
This makes faithful, useful explanation harder than explaining a single prediction in some traditional tasks.

questions.hint: At each step, the model assigns likelihoods to possible next tokens.

options.text: Choosing generated tokens according to probability distributions conditioned on the context
Selecting only a verified fact from a fixed database
Producing the same output for every prompt
Randomly choosing words without using model predictions

summary: An LLM estimates probabilities for possible next tokens and a decoding method selects one or more of them.
Sampling settings affect variation, but high probability does not establish factual correctness.

questions.questionText: What role does training data play in explainability?
questions.hint: Training data shapes what patterns a model learns, even when an exact source cannot be identified.

options.text: Its quality, coverage, and provenance influence learned behavior and what can be explained about it
It has no influence once a model has been trained
Every output can always be traced to one exact training example
It guarantees that all learned associations are fair

summary: Training data influences model capabilities, errors, and biases, so provenance and dataset documentation are important.
A generated output usually cannot be reliably attributed to one specific training item without additional evidence.

questions.hint: Uncertainty describes limits in confidence or knowledge; it is not always captured by one simple score.

options.text: A measure or indication that a model's prediction or generated answer may be unreliable or ambiguous
Proof that the model's output is false
The amount of disk space used by model weights
A guarantee that the model will refuse to answer

summary: Uncertainty signals that evidence, prediction, or interpretation may be limited or ambiguous.
Model confidence may be poorly calibrated, so uncertainty estimates should be validated for the task.

questions.questionText: Why should users understand AI limitations?
questions.hint: Knowing what a tool may get wrong helps people decide when to verify or escalate.

options.text: To use outputs appropriately, verify important claims, and seek human expertise when needed
To avoid questioning the AI once it provides an explanation
To make every task suitable for automation
To replace system testing with user awareness

summary: Users who understand limits can spot unsuitable tasks, verify high-impact claims, and apply human judgment.
Training users is valuable but does not replace building and governing the system responsibly.

questions.hint: Generated content can be persuasive while being wrong, unsafe, or unsupported.

options.text: People need ways to assess evidence, limitations, and risks behind generated content
GenAI outputs are always factual and need no scrutiny
Explainability prevents a model from generating creative content
Only non-generative models can make consequential errors

summary: Explanations help users evaluate how a generated answer was produced and what evidence supports it.
They should be paired with source checks, evaluations, and safeguards.

questions.hint: Organizations need to understand performance, control risk, and answer stakeholder questions.

options.text: To support operational oversight, compliance work, debugging, and stakeholder confidence
To avoid establishing ownership for AI systems
To guarantee that models never change
To disclose confidential data to every employee

summary: Organizations need evidence to oversee systems, understand failures, and justify uses to affected stakeholders.
Disclosure should be appropriate to each audience and protect confidential information.

questions.questionText: How does explainability support AI governance?
questions.hint: Governance requires practical oversight of how systems are built, deployed, and changed.

options.text: It provides information that helps owners monitor, review, and challenge AI behavior
It removes the need for policies and assigned owners
It proves that a system is safe under every condition
It prevents the need to document model changes

summary: Explanations, documentation, and traces give governance teams evidence for review and intervention.
Governance also needs roles, policies, risk controls, and ongoing monitoring.

questions.questionText: Why is explainability important for decision support systems?
questions.hint: A decision-maker needs to understand what evidence or factors the recommendation reflects.

options.text: It helps decision-makers assess recommendations and retain responsibility for the final decision
It automatically makes the system the final decision-maker
It eliminates the need to consider contextual information
It guarantees the recommendation is optimal

summary: Explanations let people compare recommendations with available evidence and domain context.
Decision-support systems should not obscure who has authority or responsibility.

questions.hint: People are more able to use a tool when they can understand its recommendations and limitations.

options.text: It helps users judge when outputs are relevant and when they should be checked
It forces users to accept every recommendation
It removes the need for onboarding or evaluation
It ensures that every user has identical needs

summary: Useful explanations can make system behavior easier to understand and integrate into existing work.
Adoption also depends on utility, reliability, usability, and fit with workflows.

questions.questionText: What are the legal implications of unexplained AI decisions?
questions.hint: Consider challenges in meeting duties to justify, document, or allow review of consequential decisions.

options.text: They may make it harder to demonstrate compliance, respond to challenges, or investigate harm
They automatically make every decision unlawful
They remove all legal responsibility from the organization
They always violate the same law in every jurisdiction

summary: Opacity can hinder organizations when they need to explain, document, or review a decision.
Legal duties differ by jurisdiction, sector, and use; obtain qualified advice for specific obligations.

questions.questionText: Why is explainability important in healthcare GenAI?
questions.hint: Clinical outputs can affect patient care, and clinicians need to check sources and uncertainty.

options.text: It helps clinicians assess evidence and limitations before using outputs in care
It allows a chatbot to replace clinical judgment without review
It guarantees that generated diagnoses are correct
It removes the need for patient privacy controls

summary: Healthcare explanations should help qualified professionals verify the basis and limits of an output.
They do not replace clinical validation, privacy protections, or professional responsibility.

questions.questionText: Why is explainability important in financial services?
questions.hint: Financial decisions may affect access, pricing, fraud review, or customer outcomes.

options.text: It supports review of consequential decisions, potential bias, and applicable controls
It guarantees that all customers receive identical outcomes
It eliminates the need for fraud monitoring
It makes a model's score a legally sufficient explanation in every case

summary: Financial organizations need to assess decision factors, errors, and disparate effects in context.
The explanation required depends on the product, decision, and applicable rules.

questions.questionText: How does explainability help risk management?
questions.hint: Useful explanations help identify what can fail and where controls may be needed.

options.text: It can reveal factors, assumptions, and failure patterns that inform mitigations
It removes the possibility of operational risk
It replaces incident response with model confidence scores
It guarantees that a model will not drift

summary: Explainability can help teams understand contributing factors and prioritize controls or monitoring.
Risk management remains an ongoing process, not a one-time explanation.

questions.questionText: How does explainability improve customer trust?
questions.hint: Customers should be able to understand relevant reasons and available ways to ask for review.

options.text: It can provide understandable reasons, limits, and routes to question or correct an outcome
It asks customers to trust the system without evidence
It guarantees the organization will never make an error
It conceals the use of AI from affected people

summary: Clear communication and meaningful recourse help customers understand how AI affects them.
Trust is earned through reliable behavior and accountability, not explanations alone.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between local and global explainability?
questions.hint: One focuses on an individual prediction; the other summarizes behavior across many cases.

options.text: Local explains one prediction; global summarizes general behavior across many inputs
Local summarizes the whole model; global explains one individual prediction
Both describe only the model's training process
They are different names for a model's accuracy score

summary: Local explanations describe one case, while global explanations summarize broader model behavior.
A global trend may not explain an individual result, and a local explanation may not generalize.

questions.hint: Global explanations summarize behavior across a model or a broad set of inputs.

options.text: An account of general model behavior, patterns, or important features across many cases
An explanation of only one customer's result
A list of all possible outputs for every input
A translation of a model into a single natural-language sentence

summary: Global explainability summarizes general patterns or behavior across a population or input space.
A global summary can hide important differences in particular cases.

questions.hint: This level concerns the model's design or general operation, not one decision.

options.text: Information about how a model is structured or generally behaves
A reason shown for one specific output only
A record of a single user's prompt
A measure of the model's response time

summary: Model-level explanations describe general behavior, architecture, features, or limitations.
They complement case-level explanations when users need to understand a particular result.

questions.hint: It explains an individual prediction or output in relation to its specific input.

options.text: An explanation of the factors or evidence associated with one model result
A summary of the model's architecture and training history only
A comparison of all models in a company
A guarantee that the prediction is correct

summary: Prediction-level explainability focuses on a particular model output and the input that produced it.
A plausible explanation is not proof that the prediction is accurate or fair.

questions.hint: It estimates how much input variables matter to a model, globally or for a particular prediction.

options.text: A measure or ranking of how much input features contribute to model behavior or predictions
A list of features that are legally allowed to be used
A guarantee that important features cause the outcome
A count of how many fields appear in a database

summary: Feature importance estimates the influence or contribution of inputs using a chosen method.
Importance is method-dependent and does not by itself show causation.

questions.hint: Attribution assigns some portion of an output to inputs, features, or sources.

options.text: Assigning estimated contribution to parts of an input or evidence for a model output
Assigning legal ownership of a model to its users
Encrypting the model's input features
Replacing a prediction with a rule

summary: Attribution methods estimate how input components or sources relate to a particular output.
Attribution depends on methodological choices and should not be mistaken for a causal account.

questions.hint: It concerns what people can know about the model's design, data, and operation.

options.text: The availability of relevant information about a model's design, data, behavior, and limitations
A visual display of one prediction only
The guarantee that a model has no hidden bias
The requirement to reveal private training records

summary: Model transparency provides relevant information about a model and its development or operation.
It should be balanced with privacy, security, and legitimate confidentiality.

questions.hint: This focuses on making the basis and process of a decision clear to affected people.

options.text: Clarity about how a decision was made, what factors mattered, and who is responsible
Publishing every model parameter
Showing a model's source code without explaining an outcome
Keeping a decision's criteria secret

summary: Decision transparency communicates relevant criteria, process, and responsibility for an outcome.
The appropriate detail depends on the audience and the nature of the decision.

questions.hint: It makes the basis or rationale for a system's response more visible, without assuming that text is a faithful record of internal computation.

options.text: Providing an understandable account of the considerations or evidence behind an output
Revealing every hidden neural activation to every end user
Showing a confident explanation whether or not it is accurate
Replacing evidence with a longer answer

summary: Reasoning transparency presents useful rationale, evidence, or decision steps in a form people can assess.
A generated rationale may not faithfully describe the model's internal computation.

questions.hint: Causal explanations ask what would change if a factor were intervened on, not merely correlated.

options.text: An explanation that uses cause-and-effect relationships to describe how changes may affect an outcome
A ranking of correlated features with no causal assumptions
A description of the model's training cost
A list of inputs that appeared before an output

summary: Causal explainability reasons about interventions and cause-effect relationships under stated assumptions.
Correlation or feature importance alone does not establish causation.

questions.hint: It asks how an outcome might differ under a small, meaningful change to the input.

options.text: Showing what changes to an input could have led to a different model outcome
Showing the same output repeatedly
Explaining only the model's training data
Claiming that changing a feature guarantees a real-world outcome

summary: A counterfactual describes a nearby alternative input that would change the model's prediction.
Such a model-based scenario is not necessarily a causal or feasible real-world recommendation.

questions.hint: The explanation is generated after a model has already been trained.

options.text: Methods applied to an existing trained model to explain its behavior or outputs
A model designed to be transparent by construction
A method for deleting model outputs after delivery
A guarantee that an explanation exactly matches internal computation

summary: Post-hoc methods analyze a trained model or its predictions without changing the model's basic design.
Their explanations may be approximate and should be assessed for fidelity.

questions.hint: Some models are easier to understand because their structure is transparent by design.

options.text: Interpretability that comes from the model's design, such as a small decision tree or linear model
An explanation attached to any model after training
A model whose parameters are hidden from its developers
A claim that all simple models are accurate

summary: Intrinsically interpretable models have structures people can inspect directly, such as a small rule set.
Simplicity can aid understanding but does not guarantee accuracy, fairness, or suitability.

questions.hint: Inspection examines components, behavior, or records to understand a system.

options.text: Examining a model's structure, parameters, behavior, or documentation using suitable methods
Accepting outputs without review
Changing every prediction by hand
Measuring only how quickly a model responds

summary: Model inspection uses tools and evidence to examine model components or behavior.
Inspection should be designed for the question being asked and may not reveal every internal mechanism.

questions.hint: A faithful explanation should accurately reflect the model behavior it claims to describe.

options.text: How accurately an explanation represents the behavior of the model or output it describes
How attractive an explanation looks in a dashboard
How many words an explanation contains
Whether users agree with an explanation

summary: Fidelity measures how well an explanation matches the model's actual behavior for the relevant scope.
An explanation can be easy to read yet low-fidelity, so both accuracy and usability matter.

questions.hint: It uses ideas from cooperative game theory to assign contributions to features.

options.text: A framework that assigns feature contributions to a prediction using Shapley-value ideas
A method that trains language models from scratch
A measure of model latency
A rule that guarantees causal explanations

summary: SHAP methods estimate how features contribute to a model output relative to a baseline.
The result depends on choices such as the background data and the SHAP variant used.

questions.hint: The name refers to SHapley Additive exPlanations.

options.text: SHapley Additive exPlanations
Statistical Heuristic Analysis for Predictions
Systematic Human Assessment of Probabilistic models
Secure Heuristic Attribution Protocol

summary: SHAP expands to SHapley Additive exPlanations.
It is a family of feature-attribution methods based on Shapley values.

questions.questionText: How does SHAP explain model outputs?
questions.hint: It compares feature contributions with a baseline prediction.

options.text: It estimates each feature's contribution relative to a baseline and combines contributions into the prediction
It reads the model's private thoughts as natural language
It proves that each feature causes the outcome
It replaces the model with a fixed rule

summary: SHAP values allocate a prediction difference from a baseline among input features under a chosen formulation.
They describe model attribution, not necessarily real-world causality.

questions.hint: Consider its consistent additive feature attributions and its use for both individual and overall analyses.

options.text: It provides a common additive attribution framework
It can support local explanations and aggregate global summaries
It guarantees fast computation for every model and dataset
Its assumptions and baseline can be inspected and discussed

summary: SHAP offers a principled, widely used way to attribute predictions and summarize patterns across cases.
Computation can be expensive, and results depend on the model, data, and assumptions.

questions.hint: Attributions can be costly and depend on how the baseline and feature relationships are handled.

options.text: Some variants can be computationally expensive
Attributions may be sensitive to background data and assumptions
A feature contribution automatically proves causation
Correlated features can make contributions harder to interpret

summary: SHAP can be resource-intensive and its interpretation depends on the reference distribution and feature dependence treatment.
Its attributions explain model behavior under assumptions; they are not causal proof.

questions.hint: It fits a simpler explanation around one prediction, even when the original model is complex.

options.text: Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations, a technique for approximating local model behavior
A neural network architecture for image generation
A database that stores model decisions
A metric for measuring training data volume

summary: LIME fits a simple interpretable surrogate near a particular instance to approximate a model's behavior there.
The local approximation may not reflect the model well outside the sampled neighborhood.

questions.hint: It perturbs an input, observes the model's responses, and weights nearby examples.

options.text: It samples nearby variations, queries the model, and fits a weighted simple model around the case
It retrains the original model using all possible inputs
It translates model parameters directly into verified facts
It finds the exact training example behind a prediction

summary: LIME creates perturbed samples around an input, queries the model, and weights close samples more heavily when fitting a local surrogate.
Sampling and perturbation choices can affect the explanation.

questions.hint: It is flexible and can explain one prediction without requiring direct access to model internals.

options.text: It can be used with different model types through input-output queries
Its local explanation can be represented with a simple interpretable model
It guarantees the same explanation across every run and setup
It can be applied to an individual prediction

summary: LIME is model-agnostic in common settings and provides an understandable local approximation.
Its explanations can vary with sampling and may be unreliable beyond the selected neighborhood.

questions.hint: A local surrogate depends on how the neighborhood is generated and which samples are weighted.

options.text: Results may vary with random sampling and configuration
The simple surrogate may not faithfully approximate the model
A local explanation always describes global model behavior
Perturbed samples may be unrealistic or unrepresentative

summary: LIME's sampling, neighborhood, and surrogate choices can affect fidelity and stability.
A local explanation should not be generalized to all cases without separate evaluation.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between SHAP and LIME?
questions.hint: Both can explain individual predictions, but their underlying approaches differ.

options.text: SHAP allocates contributions using Shapley-value ideas; LIME fits a weighted local surrogate around an input
SHAP is only for images, while LIME is only for text
SHAP is a training algorithm, while LIME is a database
They are identical methods with different names

summary: SHAP is based on additive feature attribution and Shapley values; LIME locally approximates behavior with a simpler model.
Both depend on assumptions and implementation choices and neither is automatically causal.

questions.hint: For an image model, they highlight pixels or regions associated with a prediction.

options.text: Visualizations that highlight input regions estimated to influence a model output
Maps showing the physical locations of model servers
A guarantee that highlighted pixels caused the prediction
A list of all images in the training set

summary: Saliency methods visualize input areas associated with a model's output, often as a heat map.
Artifacts and sensitivity to method choices mean a saliency map should not be treated as definitive evidence.

questions.hint: They display attention weights between tokens or other representations inside a transformer.

options.text: Diagrams of attention weights or patterns across model positions
A complete record of every cause behind a model output
A user-interface feature that prevents hallucinations
A chart of the model's financial costs

summary: Attention visualizations show selected attention weights or patterns in transformer layers and heads.
They reveal one part of computation but not necessarily the model's full basis for an answer.

questions.questionText: Can attention be considered an explanation?
questions.hint: Attention patterns may be informative, but researchers caution against treating them as a complete causal account.

options.text: It can provide a useful diagnostic view, but attention weights alone are not a complete or guaranteed faithful explanation
Yes; each attention weight directly measures causal importance
No; attention has no relationship to model computation
Yes; one attention map fully explains every generated token

summary: Attention can help inspect information flow, but its relationship to feature importance and causal influence is limited.
Validate explanations with other evidence and methods.

questions.hint: A simpler model is trained to approximate the behavior of a more complex model.

options.text: Interpretable models fitted to approximate a complex model's outputs or behavior
Models that replace all training data with synthetic data
Copies of model parameters used for backup
Models that guarantee the original system is correct

summary: A surrogate approximates a target model, globally or locally, using a simpler representation.
Its usefulness depends on how faithfully it represents the target over the region of interest.

questions.hint: They express a decision as human-readable conditions and outcomes.

options.text: Explanations expressed as understandable if-then rules or conditions
A neural network's hidden weights displayed as source code
A list of outputs without decision criteria
An automatic proof that a decision is fair

summary: Rules can describe conditions associated with a prediction or a decision process in readable form.
Approximate rules may omit behavior, so their coverage and fidelity should be checked.

questions.hint: They use similar, contrasting, or representative cases to make a result easier to understand.

options.text: Explanations that show relevant examples, such as similar cases or counterexamples
Explanations that publish every training record
A method that always reveals causal relationships
A numeric confidence score with no context

summary: Example-based methods explain behavior through representative, similar, or contrasting cases.
Examples must be selected carefully to avoid privacy leakage or misleading comparisons.

questions.hint: It asks whether human-understandable concepts are represented in a model's response.

options.text: Explaining model behavior using meaningful concepts rather than only raw input features
Replacing concepts with random labels
A way to train a model without any data
A guarantee that model concepts match human concepts exactly

summary: Concept-based methods relate internal representations or predictions to higher-level concepts people can understand.
The selected concepts and their measurements must be validated; alignment is not automatic.

questions.hint: It estimates how individual input features contribute to a model result.

options.text: Assigning estimated contribution values to input features for a model output
Proving which feature caused an outcome in the real world
Selecting which data fields to collect
Giving ownership of a feature to a user

summary: Feature attribution assigns estimated influence or contribution to inputs under a particular method.
Attribution describes model behavior and does not alone demonstrate causal effect.

questions.hint: They estimate how training examples might affect a model's prediction or parameters.

options.text: Techniques that estimate the effect of training data points on model behavior or a prediction
Functions that increase a model's sampling temperature
A dashboard for tracking user clicks
A guarantee that an exact training source can always be recovered

summary: Influence functions use approximations to estimate how changes to training examples may affect a model or prediction.
They can be computationally demanding and may be unreliable for some modern deep networks.

questions.hint: They bring selected explanation, evidence, and monitoring views together for users.

options.text: Interfaces that present explanation and model-monitoring information for review
A model-training algorithm that guarantees fairness
A replacement for audit processes
A system that shows predictions but hides all relevant context

summary: Dashboards organize useful information such as feature contributions, evidence, uncertainty, and performance.
They should be tailored to users and clearly communicate what the displayed explanations can and cannot establish.

questions.questionText: Why are LLMs considered black-box models?
questions.hint: Their distributed parameters and layers make a simple, faithful explanation of each response difficult.

options.text: Complex learned representations make it difficult to trace a response to a small set of understandable rules
They never use data or learned parameters
All their internal operations are ordinary human-readable rules
They always conceal outputs from their users

summary: LLMs rely on distributed representations across many parameters and computations.
Tools such as source citations or attribution reveal useful evidence, but not necessarily every internal influence.

questions.hint: It examines how input or output tokens relate to a model's next-token choices.

options.text: Analyzing how individual tokens or token positions relate to generated probabilities or outputs
Explaining a model's full training history with one token
A guarantee that each token is factually verified
Counting the words in a prompt

summary: Token-level analysis examines associations or contributions of individual tokens in a particular model computation.
It is a narrow view and does not establish the complete reason for a response.

questions.hint: It inspects attention patterns among tokens across a model's layers or heads.

options.text: Examining attention weights or patterns to study how token representations interact
Verifying every factual claim against a database
Measuring only the size of an LLM's training corpus
A method that guarantees causal explanations

summary: Attention analysis visualizes or measures parts of the information-mixing operations in transformers.
Attention patterns are informative diagnostics, not a complete explanation of an answer.

questions.hint: A clear record of instructions and context can help explain why an application elicited a response.

options.text: Making the prompt, relevant context, and instruction roles understandable and reviewable
Showing only the final response while hiding all instructions
A method that guarantees a prompt has no ambiguity
Explaining the model's training data through prompt wording

summary: Prompt explainability documents the instructions and context supplied to a model and their intended roles.
A prompt record supports investigation but does not reveal all internal model behavior.

questions.questionText: How can prompt design improve explainability?
questions.hint: Clear constraints and separated evidence make it easier to understand and evaluate what the model was asked to do.

options.text: State the task, delimit supplied data, specify evidence requirements, and request a structured result
Mix instructions and untrusted content without boundaries
Ask for confident answers without sources
Remove context and keep no record of the prompt

summary: Well-structured prompts make system behavior easier to reproduce and inspect, and can request evidence or uncertainty.
Prompt quality improves clarity but cannot guarantee correct responses.

questions.hint: It links parts of an output to the evidence, inputs, or sources that support them.

options.text: Connecting generated claims or segments to relevant input context, retrieved passages, or other evidence
Assigning a score to the model's writing style only
Proving which training sentence caused every generated word
A way to remove citations from a response

summary: Output attribution associates generated content with relevant evidence or context where that relationship can be supported.
A citation may be relevant without fully entailing the claim, so the association requires validation.

questions.questionText: How can we trace generated content?
questions.hint: Preserve a privacy-aware record of the model version, prompt, retrieved sources, and output.

options.text: Record relevant prompts, model and configuration versions, retrieval sources, tool actions, and outputs
Assume the output came from one known training example
Store user credentials in prompts for later lookup
Rely on memory instead of keeping an auditable record

summary: A trace can preserve the model version, settings, inputs, retrieved evidence, tool calls, and output needed to reconstruct a run.
Logging should minimize sensitive data and follow access and retention policies.

questions.hint: It makes visible what information was retrieved and why it was included in the response context.

options.text: Showing which sources or passages were retrieved and how they relate to the answer
Showing all documents in a company's private database to every user
Explaining only the model's attention weights
Guaranteeing that retrieval found every relevant source

summary: Retrieval explainability documents selected documents or passages, their provenance, and their link to generated claims.
It should respect access controls and does not guarantee retrieval completeness.

questions.questionText: How does Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) improve explainability?
questions.hint: RAG can ground an answer in passages that the user can inspect.

options.text: It can provide relevant retrieved evidence alongside a generated answer for checking
It makes the language model's internal reasoning fully transparent
It guarantees all retrieved documents are correct and current
It removes the need to evaluate generated claims

summary: RAG supplies retrieved context that can be cited or shown as evidence, helping users verify claims.
Retrieval can fail and the model may misrepresent sources, so both retrieval and grounding need evaluation.

questions.hint: Citations give users a route to inspect evidence behind a claim.

options.text: They let users locate and review sources associated with claims
They guarantee that every linked source supports the claim
They reveal the model's full internal computation
They make source quality irrelevant

summary: Citations provide a path to inspect source material and can make provenance clearer.
Citations must be checked for accuracy, relevance, and whether the source actually supports the statement.

questions.hint: Grounding connects a response to evidence rather than relying only on fluent generation.

options.text: It helps users verify that claims are supported by relevant, accessible evidence
It guarantees the model will never make an unsupported inference
It allows the system to ignore source dates and quality
It proves that a response is unbiased

summary: Source grounding helps connect generated claims to evidence that a reviewer can inspect.
It reduces some risks but cannot guarantee source completeness, accuracy, or faithful use.

questions.hint: A concise sequence of intermediate steps may make a task's approach easier to inspect.

options.text: It may present intermediate steps that help users inspect the approach to a task
It always reveals a faithful record of internal model computation
It proves that the final answer is correct
It removes the need for evidence or external verification

summary: A stepwise account can expose assumptions or intermediate results for checking.
A model-generated reasoning trace can be incomplete or post-hoc and should not be treated as ground truth.

questions.questionText: What are the limitations of chain-of-thought explanations?
questions.hint: A plausible verbal rationale may not match the computations that actually shaped the answer.

options.text: The trace may not faithfully represent internal computation
A persuasive trace may still contain errors
Longer reasoning always makes an answer correct
Detailed traces can expose sensitive information or enable misuse

summary: Chain-of-thought text may be unfaithful, incorrect, or unnecessarily disclose sensitive details.
Use appropriate evidence, concise rationales, and validation rather than assuming a reasoning trace proves correctness.

questions.hint: Explanation methods can approximate behavior, and generated rationales can be plausible but unfaithful.

options.text: Yes; explanations can omit factors, misstate evidence, or poorly approximate model behavior
No; any explanation produced by an AI is inherently true
No; a fluent explanation proves its own accuracy
Only explanations written by humans can be inaccurate

summary: Explanations are claims that need evaluation: they may be incomplete, unstable, or inconsistent with model behavior.
Validate them against the system, evidence, and the decision context.

questions.questionText: How should AI-generated explanations be validated?
questions.hint: Check the explanation against sources, model behavior, and expert review rather than trusting its fluency.

options.text: Test fidelity and stability, verify cited evidence, and obtain domain review where appropriate
Accept the explanation whenever it sounds confident
Compare only its length with the original output
Ask the same model to confirm its explanation and stop there

summary: Validation can measure fidelity, stability, usefulness, and agreement with evidence or expert judgment.
A model's self-confirmation alone is not independent verification.

questions.questionText: Why is explainability important for AI agents?
questions.hint: Agents can take multiple steps and cause real effects through tools.

options.text: People need to understand the agent's plan, tool use, decisions, and resulting actions
Agents never affect external systems
Explainability allows an agent to bypass permissions
A final answer fully describes every action an agent took

summary: Agents can plan, call tools, and take actions, so their decisions and side effects need traceable explanations.
Human and system controls should remain in place for consequential actions.

questions.questionText: How do autonomous agents make decisions?
questions.hint: They use goals, current context, observations, policies, and available actions to choose a next step.

options.text: They evaluate context and goals, select an action, observe its result, and may update their plan
They make decisions without any input or system configuration
They always follow a single fixed script regardless of feedback
They act only after a human writes every tool call

summary: An agent commonly combines a goal, model, instructions, observations, and available actions in an action-feedback loop.
The application should constrain which actions are available and when approval is required.

questions.questionText: How can agent reasoning be explained?
questions.hint: Record concise rationales along with the plan, evidence, decisions, and outcomes.

options.text: Provide a trace of goals, selected steps, evidence, tool results, and decision rationales
Show only the final answer and delete all intermediate records
Publish hidden credentials used by the agent
Assume a generated chain of thought is a complete audit record

summary: An agent trace can record its plan, relevant evidence, tool calls, results, approvals, and outcomes.
A concise action rationale is more dependable for auditing than treating private model reasoning as a perfect transcript.

questions.hint: Make clear which tool was called, with what authorized inputs, and what it returned.

options.text: Making tool selection, validated arguments, execution status, and results visible to appropriate reviewers
Allowing tools to run without logging or authorization
Showing a tool's name but concealing all relevant activity
Giving the model unrestricted access to every tool

summary: Tool-call transparency provides an inspectable record of what action was requested, validated, executed, and returned.
Sensitive arguments and results still require appropriate access controls.

questions.questionText: Why should agent actions be logged?
questions.hint: Logs can help reconstruct what happened during debugging, incident review, or an audit.

options.text: To reconstruct actions, investigate failures, verify authorization, and support oversight
To retain all personal data forever
To make the agent's actions impossible to challenge
To replace validation before executing tools

summary: Action logs support debugging, monitoring, accountability, and incident investigation.
Logging should be proportionate, protected, and governed by retention and privacy rules.

questions.hint: Traceability connects a request to the action an agent took and what happened next.

options.text: The ability to follow an agent action from its initiating request through execution and outcome
The ability to generate an unlimited number of actions
A measure of how many tools an agent knows about
A way to hide an agent's tool activity

summary: Action traceability links intent, chosen tool, validated inputs, approval, execution, and result.
This helps determine whether an action was authorized and what impact it had.

questions.questionText: How do agents use external tools?
questions.hint: A model proposes a structured call, while the application should control and validate execution.

options.text: An agent selects an allowed tool and proposes arguments that the application validates and executes
The model should receive raw production credentials and run any code
Tools automatically know the user's goal without arguments
Every tool result is trusted without validation

summary: Agents may request a tool call; application code should enforce schemas, permissions, and execution policy.
Tool results are external inputs and should be checked before they influence later actions.

questions.questionText: Why should external data sources be explainable?
questions.hint: People need to know where information came from and whether it was current and trustworthy.

options.text: Provenance and quality help reviewers judge whether an agent's evidence is relevant and reliable
External data is always more accurate than internal data
A source name guarantees the content is current
Data lineage is unnecessary once a model uses a tool

summary: Source provenance, timestamp, access path, and quality help reviewers interpret evidence used by an agent.
External sources may be stale, incomplete, or untrusted and need appropriate validation.

questions.hint: It covers how an overall process flows through steps, decisions, tools, and handoffs.

options.text: Making workflow stages, decision points, dependencies, and outcomes understandable
Explaining only one model parameter
Showing the final result without any process information
A guarantee that workflows never fail

summary: Workflow explainability makes the sequence and control points of a process visible to reviewers.
It helps identify where an error, delay, or unauthorized action occurred.

questions.hint: ReAct interleaves reasoning-oriented steps with actions and observations.

options.text: It structures agent behavior around reasoning, actions, and observations that can be traced
It removes the need to log tool calls
It guarantees every reasoning trace is faithful
It is a method for training image classifiers

summary: ReAct combines reasoning-oriented steps with actions and observations, making the interaction cycle easier to inspect.
Visible traces do not guarantee correctness and should be designed with privacy and safety in mind.

questions.hint: The name refers to Reasoning WithOut Observation, a pattern that plans tool use before execution.

options.text: An agent approach that separates planning from tool execution and later combines tool results
A database protocol for storing model weights
A method that requires the model to observe every tool result before planning
A technique for explaining feature importance

summary: ReWOO (Reasoning WithOut Observation) separates a plan from tool execution, allowing tool calls to be prepared and run before results are integrated.
The structure can reduce repeated model calls but may need recovery when results differ from expectations.

questions.questionText: How is ReWOO different from ReAct?
questions.hint: Compare interleaved action-observation loops with planning first and observing tool results later.

options.text: ReAct commonly alternates reasoning and observations; ReWOO separates planning from tool execution and later uses results
ReWOO never uses tools, while ReAct only uses tools
ReAct is a database; ReWOO is a neural network layer
There is no difference in their workflow patterns

summary: ReAct typically iterates through action and observation steps, while ReWOO plans tool calls before incorporating their outputs.
Each pattern has trade-offs in adaptability, latency, and handling unexpected observations.

questions.questionText: How can multi-agent systems remain explainable?
questions.hint: Record each agent's role, handoffs, inputs, outputs, and decisions in a shared trace.

options.text: Define agent responsibilities and log handoffs, evidence, decisions, tool calls, and outcomes
Let agents communicate through unrecorded channels
Hide which agent produced each result
Assume consensus among agents proves correctness

summary: Clear roles and end-to-end traces make contributions and handoffs between agents reviewable.
Agreement among agents is not independent proof because they may share data, models, or failure modes.

questions.hint: It explains how an orchestrator assigns work and coordinates participating agents or tools.

options.text: Visibility into how tasks are routed, agents are selected, and their results are combined
Giving each agent unrestricted authority
Showing only the final response from a system
A method for increasing model parameter counts

summary: Orchestration transparency describes task routing, delegation rules, permissions, and how outputs are combined.
These details help reviewers identify gaps, conflicts, and responsibility.

questions.questionText: How do audit trails support explainability?
questions.hint: An audit trail is a sequence of records that can reconstruct actions and changes.

options.text: They preserve a reviewable history of inputs, decisions, approvals, actions, and outcomes
They guarantee that recorded decisions were fair
They replace the need to control access to logs
They store only model confidence and no other context

summary: Audit trails provide evidence for reconstructing how a system operated and who approved consequential actions.
Records must be accurate, protected from tampering, and retained appropriately.

questions.hint: It prompts a model to produce intermediate steps before or while giving a final answer.

options.text: A prompting approach that asks a model to work through intermediate reasoning steps
A cryptographic chain that stores training examples
A guarantee that all intermediate statements are correct
A method for retrieving current web pages

summary: Chain-of-thought prompting asks a model to produce stepwise intermediate content for a task.
The produced text is not necessarily a faithful or complete record of internal computations.

questions.hint: Intermediate steps can make assumptions or calculations easier to inspect.

options.text: It can expose intermediate steps that a reviewer may check for errors or assumptions
It guarantees faithful access to a model's hidden reasoning
It ensures that every output is evidence-based
It eliminates the need for external validation

summary: A stepwise response can help a reviewer inspect an approach, identify a faulty step, or ask for supporting evidence.
A chain of thought is not, by itself, proof of correctness or internal faithfulness.

questions.questionText: How does CoT improve reasoning quality?
questions.hint: Breaking a complex task into explicit stages can help a model organize intermediate calculations.

options.text: It can encourage decomposition into intermediate steps that are easier to evaluate
It guarantees flawless reasoning for every task
It supplies missing facts from verified sources automatically
It prevents errors caused by ambiguous instructions

summary: Stepwise prompting may improve performance on some tasks by encouraging structured decomposition.
Benefits are task-dependent and should be measured; the method does not guarantee correctness.

questions.hint: They are the supporting substeps between a task's input and final result.

options.text: Subtasks, calculations, or decisions presented between the input and final answer
The final answer repeated with different wording
Model parameters that users always see directly
External sources that are retrieved after a response

summary: Intermediate steps describe a sequence of subproblems or calculations used to reach a result.
When exposed, they are generated content and may need independent checking.

questions.hint: Visible steps may show where a calculation, assumption, or inference went wrong.

options.text: It can help reviewers locate questionable assumptions or steps in a task solution
It identifies every bug in a system automatically
It replaces logs, tests, and reproducible examples
It prevents a model from making mistakes

summary: Intermediate output can make some failures easier to localize and reproduce.
Debugging still needs independent checks, system logs, and tests because the trace may omit the true cause.

questions.hint: A model may review or critique an earlier output, but that review is not automatically objective.

options.text: A process in which a model evaluates or revises its own earlier response or plan
A guarantee of independent expert review
A method for encrypting the model's memory
A type of human oversight that requires no people

summary: Self-reflection asks a model to inspect, critique, or revise a prior output.
The same model can repeat or reinforce its own errors, so important checks should use independent evidence or reviewers.

questions.hint: Generate multiple reasoning paths and compare their final answers.

options.text: Sampling multiple candidate reasoning paths and selecting an answer based on agreement or another decision rule
Running one model output once and assuming it is correct
Combining outputs from unrelated tasks without comparison
A way to guarantee independent opinions from identical model calls

summary: Self-consistency samples multiple candidate solutions and uses their agreement to select or assess an answer.
Candidates may share systematic errors, so agreement is a signal rather than proof.

questions.hint: Review the recorded sequence of steps and evidence rather than looking only at the final answer.

options.text: Examining a sequence of recorded reasoning-oriented steps, actions, and evidence for patterns or errors
Reading only the final output and discarding its context
A technique that proves hidden reasoning is fully visible
Measuring only how long a model took to respond

summary: Trace analysis reviews a system's recorded steps, evidence, and actions to understand behavior or diagnose failures.
A trace may be incomplete and should be interpreted alongside system behavior and logs.

questions.hint: Some internal model processes are not directly observable, and generated rationales may not faithfully represent them.

options.text: Internal computation may be inaccessible, while verbal rationales can be incomplete or unfaithful
Hidden reasoning always makes a model accurate
A visible rationale always exposes every model operation
The model's private reasoning can be reconstructed exactly from its final answer

summary: Neural computations are not necessarily represented by the text an LLM produces as a rationale.
Treat explanations as evidence to test, not direct transcripts of hidden cognition.

questions.questionText: Should internal reasoning always be exposed?
questions.hint: Balance usefulness with fidelity, privacy, security, and the needs of the user.

options.text: No; provide appropriate evidence and concise rationales while considering safety, privacy, and fidelity
Yes; every internal token must be published to every user
Yes; exposing reasoning guarantees correctness
No; never provide any explanation or evidence

summary: Exposing raw reasoning is not always useful, safe, faithful, or appropriate.
A well-designed system can offer evidence, concise rationales, uncertainty, and audit records suited to each audience.

questions.hint: Trustworthiness includes reliability and safeguards throughout a system's lifecycle.

options.text: AI designed and operated to be reliable, safe, fair, transparent, and accountable in context
AI that users are told never to question
Any model with high accuracy on one test
AI whose source code is public, regardless of behavior

summary: Trustworthy AI is designed and governed to meet relevant expectations such as reliability, safety, fairness, and accountability.
No single property or label proves that a system is trustworthy in every context.

questions.hint: It includes responsible choices from design and data collection through deployment and monitoring.

options.text: Developing and using AI with attention to its impacts, risks, rights, and accountability
Using AI only when it produces a high-confidence output
A tool that automatically makes ethical decisions
Publishing every dataset regardless of consent

summary: Responsible AI applies principles and controls across development, deployment, and use to manage impacts and risks.
It requires human and organizational accountability, not just technical features.

questions.hint: Fairness concerns how people and groups are treated, and the appropriate measure depends on context.

options.text: Treating people justly under relevant ethical and legal criteria, assessed in context
Giving every person identical predictions regardless of relevant circumstances
A single universal metric that fits every AI task
Removing every feature that could correlate with a protected trait

summary: Fairness concerns equitable treatment and outcomes under context-specific principles and legal requirements.
Different fairness goals can conflict, so the chosen criteria and trade-offs should be justified.

questions.hint: Explanations can expose which factors influence decisions and how those factors behave across groups.

options.text: It can help reviewers investigate decision factors and compare outcomes across relevant groups
It guarantees equal outcomes without measurement
It removes the need for representative evaluation data
It proves that any feature attribution is a causal explanation

summary: Explanations can help identify concerning features or patterns for further fairness testing.
Fairness requires appropriate group metrics, data analysis, and context; explanations alone do not prove fairness.

questions.hint: Bias can enter through data, labels, design choices, deployment, or social context.

options.text: A systematic pattern that can produce distorted or unfair outcomes in a model or its use
Any difference between two individual predictions
A random software crash
A guarantee that model outputs are inaccurate

summary: AI bias can arise from systematic patterns in data, labels, modeling choices, or deployment context that lead to problematic outcomes.
Not every group difference has the same cause or remedy; investigate the specific setting.

questions.hint: Compare influential factors and explanation patterns across groups, then test outcomes with suitable metrics.

options.text: They can highlight suspicious decision factors or differing patterns that warrant fairness investigation
They automatically prove a system is unbiased
They replace evaluation across demographic groups
They guarantee that removing a sensitive feature removes all bias

summary: Explanations can surface proxies or group-specific patterns that guide further investigation.
Bias may remain through correlated features or system design, so conduct broader fairness testing.

questions.hint: Ethical use considers impacts on people and society, not just technical performance.

options.text: AI developed and used in ways that consider human values, rights, harms, and responsibilities
AI that is ethical because it is automated
AI that optimizes accuracy without considering impacts
A model that has no human owners

summary: Ethical AI considers values, rights, harms, benefits, and responsibilities in its design and use.
Ethical decisions require context and accountable people; they cannot be delegated entirely to a model.

questions.hint: Oversight gives people a meaningful ability to supervise and intervene.

options.text: Arrangements that let qualified people monitor, review, correct, or stop an AI system
A person who merely watches a dashboard with no authority
Allowing a model to approve its own decisions
Removing humans from consequential workflows

summary: Human oversight gives responsible people the knowledge, authority, and practical ability to intervene.
A nominal human check is ineffective if reviewers lack context, time, or power to act.

questions.hint: Humans can review exceptions and consequential outcomes, provided they have meaningful authority and information.

options.text: It enables human judgment, correction, and escalation when automated outputs need review
It guarantees that every human reviewer is unbiased
It removes the need to design safe systems
It means humans must manually approve every low-risk computation

summary: Human-in-the-Loop arrangements can provide review and intervention for uncertain or consequential cases.
They must be designed carefully to avoid rubber-stamping and should match the level of risk.

questions.questionText: What role do humans play in explainability?
questions.hint: People interpret explanations, compare them with evidence, and decide what action is appropriate.

options.text: They assess whether explanations are useful, accurate, and appropriate and act on concerns
They accept every explanation without question
They transfer accountability to the model
They need no domain knowledge to review high-impact decisions

summary: People determine how explanations fit a decision, challenge unsupported claims, and trigger correction or escalation.
Reviewers need appropriate training, evidence, and authority.

questions.hint: Governance defines who gets explanations, what quality they need, and how those explanations are monitored.

options.text: Policies and responsibilities for designing, validating, delivering, and monitoring AI explanations
A technique that automatically generates perfect explanations
A requirement to publish all model internals
A practice limited to choosing chart colors

summary: Explainability governance establishes roles, standards, access, evaluation, and processes for explanation quality.
It helps ensure explanations are appropriate for users and decision contexts.

questions.hint: A useful record helps identify who approved a system and what evidence informed a decision.

options.text: They help people inspect decision factors and connect outcomes to responsible roles and controls
They make the AI model legally responsible instead of its operator
They remove the need to document ownership
They guarantee that no one will dispute a decision

summary: Explanations and records can clarify the basis of decisions and support investigation of responsible processes.
Accountability still requires named owners, authority, and remedies.

questions.hint: An auditable system leaves enough reliable evidence for authorized reviewers to examine it.

options.text: The ability to examine evidence, records, and controls about an AI system and its decisions
A guarantee that an audit will find no issues
The publication of every user record
A model's ability to explain itself in fluent language

summary: Auditability means reviewers can access reliable evidence about system design, operation, decisions, and controls.
Records should be sufficient for oversight while protecting privacy and security.

questions.hint: A decision should have an understandable, reviewable basis and a clear responsible owner.

options.text: Making decisions with understandable reasons, relevant evidence, and a process for review
Accepting an AI score without considering context
Using explanations as a substitute for evidence
Allowing a system to make decisions with no accountable owner

summary: Explainable decision-making communicates reasons and evidence so that decisions can be evaluated and challenged.
The explanation should match the actual process and leave room for correction.

questions.hint: Documentation, traceability, and explanations can provide evidence for required oversight.

options.text: It can help provide decision records and evidence for reviews required by applicable rules
It guarantees compliance with every law
It replaces legal and policy analysis
It requires disclosure of all confidential information

summary: XAI can support compliance by improving documentation, reviewability, and evidence of controls.
It does not itself satisfy legal requirements; obligations must be assessed for the use and jurisdiction.

questions.hint: It covers the roles, policies, and controls used to oversee AI throughout its lifecycle.

options.text: The structures, policies, responsibilities, and controls for managing AI systems and their risks
A single accuracy metric for a model
A process performed only after an AI incident
A technique for increasing model size

summary: AI governance defines how organizations direct, oversee, and control AI development and use.
Effective governance spans the lifecycle and assigns clear responsibilities.

questions.questionText: Why must AI decisions be auditable?
questions.hint: Records enable authorized people to reconstruct, review, and challenge consequential decisions.

options.text: To investigate outcomes, verify controls, and demonstrate how decisions were reached
To make every internal record public
To guarantee no decision will be challenged
To avoid assigning system owners

summary: Auditability provides evidence for accountability, incident response, and review of decisions.
Auditing requires trustworthy, appropriately protected records.

questions.hint: Guardrails constrain system behavior and support safe, policy-compliant use.

options.text: Controls that limit or guide AI inputs, outputs, and actions according to policy
A guarantee that a model cannot fail
A way to remove all human review
A list of model capabilities without operational controls

summary: Guardrails include rules, validation, permissions, filters, and escalation steps that constrain system behavior.
They reduce risk but must be tested and monitored because they can fail.

questions.hint: Clear controls make it easier to understand why an action was allowed, blocked, or escalated.

options.text: They define reviewable rules and log when a request triggers an allow, block, or escalation
They reveal every parameter in a model automatically
They guarantee all explanations are faithful
They hide policy decisions from users

summary: Documented guardrails make system boundaries and intervention points clearer to reviewers.
Logging outcomes and reasons can support explanation, but controls do not expose all model internals.

questions.hint: Explanations themselves can mislead, disclose sensitive details, or be used inappropriately.

options.text: The risk that explanations are inaccurate, misleading, unstable, or disclose sensitive information
A guarantee that model explanations are complete
The risk that a model responds too quickly
A synonym for model accuracy

summary: Explanation risk includes false confidence, low fidelity, inconsistent results, and privacy or security leakage.
Explanation methods need validation and access controls like other system components.

questions.hint: They document a model's intended uses, evaluation, limitations, and performance context.

options.text: Structured documents describing a model's purpose, evaluation, limitations, and appropriate use
Physical cards that store model parameters
A guarantee of regulatory approval
A list of customer passwords used in training
